# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic, pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy that remains an important cause of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide. PPCM is a form of systolic heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction affecting childbearing women during pregnancy or in the early postpartum period; delays in diagnosis may occur because its symptoms and signs can mimic the normal findings of late pregnancy, and while some women have relatively mild disease and complete recovery, others experience significant morbidity and mortality [1]. The first formal case definition was established by a National Institutes of Health workshop, requiring heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, absence of another identifiable cause, and absence of recognizable heart disease before the last month of pregnancy [2]. The most widely used contemporary definition derives from the 2010 position statement of the Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group on PPCM [3], which characterizes PPCM as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with left ventricular systolic dysfunction, generally with an ejection fraction below 45%, and emphasizes that it is a diagnosis of exclusion [4].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography and ethnicity, reflecting socioeconomic and genetic influences [5]. From 2004 to 2011, the incidence of PPCM increased in the United States, with a study of 34 219 women aged 15 to 54 years finding an overall PPCM rate of 10.3 per 10 000 (about 1 in 968) live births [6]. Incidence is lowest in the West and highest in the South, and women with chronic hypertension have a substantially higher incidence than those without [6]. In high-burden regions of sub-Saharan Africa, reported rates are considerably higher, approaching 1 in 1000 live births [7].

## Pathophysiology

The cause of PPCM is multifactorial and incompletely understood, but a central unifying concept is the "vascular-hormonal hypothesis." In a landmark study, female mice with cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of STAT3 developed PPCM; cardiac cathepsin D expression and activity were enhanced and associated with generation of a cleaved antiangiogenic and proapoptotic 16-kDa form of the nursing hormone prolactin, and treatment with bromocriptine prevented disease [8]. Soluble Fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1) was sufficient to cause profound systolic dysfunction in mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α; sFlt1 levels are markedly elevated in preeclampsia, helping explain why preeclampsia is a strong risk factor, and elevated sFlt1 has been found in women with PPCM and predicts worse outcomes [9]. This angiogenic imbalance is supported by clinical biomarker data from prospective cohorts [10]. Disrupted metabolic homeostasis in the heart owing to pregnancy-induced hormone fluctuations is also implicated [11], and microRNA-146a has been identified as both a mediator and biomarker [12].

A genetic predisposition is now firmly established. Among 172 women with PPCM, 26 distinct rare truncating variants were identified in eight genes; the prevalence of truncating variants (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population but similar to a dilated cardiomyopathy cohort, with two-thirds in TTN [13]. An earlier Dutch study likewise found titin mutations common in families with both PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy [14]. A subsequent study provided the first extensive genetic and phenotypic landscape of PPCM, confirming that predisposition to heart failure is an important risk factor and that PPCM occurs in approximately 1 in 2000 deliveries [15], reinforcing recommendations for genetic testing analogous to dilated cardiomyopathy [16].

## Diagnosis

PPCM is idiopathic heart failure occurring in the absence of determinable heart disease, and diagnostic echocardiographic criteria include a left ventricular ejection fraction below 0.45 or fractional shortening below 30% [17]. A high index of suspicion is required because shortness of breath, fatigue and leg oedema are common in the peripartum period [18]. Natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging assist in diagnosis and exclusion of alternative etiologies [17,19]. Reversal of inflammatory and oxidative markers such as interferon-γ, oxidized LDL, and prolactin has been shown to correlate with clinical improvement [20].

## Management

Treatment combines guideline-directed heart failure therapy with disease-specific considerations and a multidisciplinary approach [18]. In a single-centre, randomized, open-label, proof-of-concept pilot study, 10 women received standard care and 10 received standard care plus bromocriptine for 8 weeks, with significantly fewer bromocriptine-treated patients meeting a composite end point of poor outcome at 6 months [21]. A subsequent multicentre trial randomized 63 PPCM patients with ejection fraction ≤35% to short-term or long-term bromocriptine [22], and demonstrated that prolactin inhibition added to standard therapy was associated with a high recovery rate and very low rate of adverse outcome [22]. The biological rationale for prolactin blockade was articulated early after the Cell study [23], and bromocriptine is now incorporated into ESC guidance, though anticoagulation is advised given the prothrombotic milieu [18]. Devices and advanced therapies, including mechanical circulatory support and transplantation, are reserved for refractory cases [24].

## Outcomes and Prognosis

Recovery is more frequent in PPCM than in other recent-onset cardiomyopathies [25]. In the prospective multicentre IPAC study, event-free survival at 1 year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% of patients achieved an ejection fraction of 50% or greater [26]. A lower baseline ejection fraction was associated with more improvement, although outcomes were worse in women presenting with very low ejection fraction and varied by race [26]. Comparisons have shown differences in clinical characteristics and outcomes between African American and non-African American women [27]. The ESC EORP global registry has further described contemporary presentation, management, and 6-month outcomes across diverse settings [28].

## Subsequent Pregnancy

Counseling regarding future pregnancies is essential. Through a survey, 44 women with prior PPCM had 60 subsequent pregnancies; among first subsequent pregnancies, 28 occurred in women whose left ventricular function had normalized and 16 in women with persistent dysfunction [29], with worse maternal and fetal outcomes among those with persistent dysfunction. A meta-analysis of 29 studies involving 779 women found the risk of cardiac failure relapse in the first subsequent pregnancy was 32%, and was higher among women with non-recovered (36%) than recovered (24%) cardiac function [30].

## Conclusion

PPCM is a heterogeneous disorder driven by an interplay of vascular-hormonal toxicity and genetic susceptibility. Advances in understanding its pathophysiology have yielded disease-specific therapy with bromocriptine and improved prognostic stratification, yet substantial global inequities in outcomes persist, and prospective trials and registries remain essential to refine management.
